pages.x: In the 1840s Ireland, ruled from London since 1801, had about eight and a half million people. Most were poor tenants on small plots, and about a third of them lived almost wholly on potatoes. In September 1845 a blight, a mould from America, turned the crop black and rotten in the ground.

The blight came back year after year. 1847, remembered as Black '47, was the worst: families died of hunger and of the fevers that came with it, in their cabins, on the roads and in crowded workhouses. In Skibbereen, in County Cork, visitors found whole villages of the dead and dying.

Even in the worst years ships carried grain, cattle and butter out of Ireland, sold to those who could pay. The British government believed the market should be left alone. It closed its soup kitchens after a few months in 1847 and left relief to local taxes and workhouses. Charles Trevelyan, who ran it, called the famine a judgement of God.

In 1847 the Choctaw Nation, driven from its own land on the Trail of Tears only 16 years before, collected 170 dollars for the starving Irish. Gifts came from around the world, from the Ottoman sultan to people in Calcutta. In 2017 a sculpture of nine steel feathers was unveiled in County Cork to say thank you.

Between 1845 and 1852 about a million people died. A million or more left on crowded, fever-ridden ships, the coffin ships, for Britain, Canada and the United States. Landlords evicted tens of thousands of families who could not pay their rent, and knocked down their cabins so they could not come back.

pages.x: The leaving never stopped. Ireland's people fell from 8.5 million to about 6.5 million in ten years, and kept falling for a century: the island still has fewer people today than it had in 1841. The Irish built new lives in Boston, New York, Liverpool and Sydney, and tens of millions around the world now have Irish roots.

The famine changed Ireland for ever. It emptied the countryside, made emigration a way of life and left a bitterness toward British rule that fed the struggle for independence. Every year Ireland holds a day to remember the Great Hunger, and it gives generously to fight famine elsewhere.
